table.caption: Typical reproductive traits of four animal species (invented values for practice, in realistic ranges)

r-k-selection-s2.title: Two ways to come back
r-k-selection-s2.passage: After a hard winter, the vole population in a northern meadow fell from about 200 per hectare to 10. By the end of the next summer it was back above 150: a female vole can breed at a few weeks old and raise several litters a year. In the same region, commercial whaling from the 1800s to the early 1900s cut bowhead whales to a few thousand animals. Bowheads begin breeding at about 25 years old and have one calf every three or four years, after a pregnancy of over a year. Even with protection from commercial hunting since the 1930s, the western Arctic population took most of a century to grow back to more than 10,000. A species’ way of reproducing, the authors argue, decides how quickly it can make up for losses, and should shape how much hunting or fishing it can take.
r-k-selection-s2.source: Invented passage for practice, based on the general biology of voles and on NOAA Fisheries facts about bowhead whales.

items.q: Which species in the table shows the most K-selected traits?
options: Gorilla
Field mouse
Pond frog
Albatross and pond frog equally

why.correct: K-selected: few offspring, late breeding, long care, long life.
options: Right: very few offspring, late first breeding, about 4 years of care and a long life.
Many offspring, very early breeding and a short life are r-selected traits.
Thousands of offspring and no care are r-selected traits.
The frog’s traits are strongly r-selected; the two are not alike.

items.q: Which species in the table gives its offspring the least parental care?
options: Field mouse
Pond frog
Gorilla
Albatross

why.correct: Little or no care is an r-selected trait.
options: Mice nurse their young for a few weeks.
Right: the table lists no care at all for the frog.
Gorillas care for their young for about 4 years.
Albatrosses care for their chick for about a year.

items.q: If a field mouse lives its typical life span, how many offspring does it produce, using the table’s values?

why.correct: Offspring per year times years of life: $30\,\frac{\text{offspring}}{\text{yr}} \times 1\,\text{yr} = 30$ offspring. (A slightly more careful count would subtract the first 0.2 years before it can breed.)

mistakes.why: That multiplies by 0.2, the age at first breeding. Use the life span, 1 year.
That adds the numbers. Multiply offspring per year by years of life.

items.q: Which species would most likely rebound fastest after a flood kills 90% of its population?
options: Gorilla
Albatross
Field mouse
They would rebound equally fast

why.correct: Early breeding and many offspring mean fast recovery.
options: One young every four years and breeding at 10 make recovery slow.
One chick every two years and breeding at 8 make recovery slow.
Right: breeding at a few months old and raising many young a year gives it a very high biotic potential.
Their reproductive traits differ greatly, so their recovery speeds differ.

items.q: What is the main claim of the passage?
options: Voles are more valuable to the meadow than whales are to the sea
Hard winters are worse for voles than hunting was for whales
Bowhead whales are no longer protected from hunting
How a species reproduces sets how fast it recovers and how much harvest it can take

why.correct: The final sentence states the claim the two examples support.
options: The passage compares recovery, not value.
The passage does not rank the two events by harm.
The passage says they have been protected since the 1930s.
Right: the last sentence states this, and the voles and whales illustrate it.

items.q: Which evidence from the passage best supports the claim that the whales recover slowly?
options: They first breed at about 25 and calve each 3 to 4 years
Whaling cut them to a few thousand
They live in the same northern region as the voles do
They have been protected since the 1930s

why.correct: Recovery speed comes from reproductive traits.
options: Right: late breeding and few offspring explain slow recovery.
That explains why they fell, not why recovery is slow.
Location does not explain the speed of recovery.
Protection allows recovery; it does not explain its pace.

items.q: Which harvest rule fits the passage’s argument best?
options: Take an equal share of each species each year
Take a smaller share each year from slow-reproducing species
Take more from species that live longer, since there are more old animals
Stop counting populations once a species is protected

why.correct: K-selected species can sustain only light harvests.
options: The passage argues that different reproductive strategies need different limits.
Right: species that replace losses slowly can sustain only small harvests.
Long-lived, slow-breeding species are the ones that recover slowly.
Counting is how a recovery like the whales’ is tracked.

items.q: Which set of traits describes an r-selected species?
options: Few large offspring, much care, late breeding
Many offspring, much care, late breeding
Many small offspring, little care, early breeding
Few offspring, no care, long life

why.correct: r-selected: many, small, little care, early, short-lived.
options: These are K-selected traits.
Much care and late breeding are K-selected traits.
Right: all three are r-selected traits.
Few offspring and a long life are K-selected traits.
The largest number of different species an area can hold
The number of offspring that survive to adulthood
The total mass of the living things in an area
The fastest growth a population could reach with no limits

why.correct: High biotic potential: many offspring, early and often.
options: That would describe species richness, not biotic potential.
Biotic potential is the fastest possible growth, not actual survival.
That is biomass.
Right: it is the fastest possible growth, set by reproductive traits.

items.q: Explain why mosquito populations often bounce back within weeks after a spraying program ends.

why.correct: Name the r-selected traits, then the rebound.

specific.frame: Mosquitoes ___, so the few that survive ___, which ___.

cause.label: Strategy
options: are r-selected, laying many eggs and maturing within days
are K-selected, raising one young at a time
live many years and breed late

why.1: Mosquitoes lay hundreds of eggs; they are not K-selected.
why.2: Mosquitoes live weeks and breed within days.

effect.label: Survivors
options: can each produce hundreds of offspring quickly
need years to produce one offspring
stop breeding until spraying returns

mechanism.label: Result
options: lets the population increase rapidly back to its earlier size
keeps the population low for decades
makes the population smaller each year

why.2: High biotic potential drives the population up, not down.

specific.model: Mosquitoes are r-selected, laying many eggs and maturing within days, so the few that survive can each produce hundreds of offspring quickly, which lets the population increase rapidly back to its earlier size.

items.q: Which traits are typical of K-selected species? Select all that apply.
options: Large offspring that receive a lot of parental care
Long life spans and late first reproduction
Populations that swing sharply up and down
Thousands of offspring each season

why.correct: K-selected: few, large, cared for, long-lived.
options: Right: K-selected species invest heavily in each offspring.
Right: both are K-selected traits.
Sharp swings are typical of r-selected species.
Thousands of offspring is r-selected.

items.q: Why are K-selected species, such as large whales and great apes, more likely than r-selected species to become threatened when people hunt them?
options: They replace losses slowly, so hunting outpaces births
They are smaller and easier to catch than most r-selected species
They live in more habitats than r-selected species
They produce more offspring than hunters can find

why.correct: Slow reproduction means slow recovery from any extra deaths.
options: Right: few offspring, late breeding and long gaps between births mean slow recovery.
Whales and great apes are large; size is not the reason.
Habitat range is not what makes K-selected species vulnerable.
They produce few offspring, which is the problem.

items.q: Dandelions produce hundreds of wind-blown seeds, flower within months, and quickly cover bare ground after it is cleared. How would you classify them?
options: Mainly K-selected
Mainly r-selected
Neither, because plants have no reproductive strategy
K-selected, because their seeds have no parental care

why.correct: Weeds that colonize bare ground are classic r-selected species.
options: K-selected plants, such as oaks, grow slowly and reproduce late.
Right: many small seeds, early reproduction and fast spread onto open ground are r-selected traits.
Plants have reproductive strategies too; trees and weeds differ greatly.
No parental care is an r-selected trait.

items.q: Sea turtles lay about 100 eggs per nest and leave them, but they live 50 or more years and first breed at 20 to 30. How are they best described?
options: Purely r-selected, because they lay many eggs
Purely K-selected, because they live long
A mix of r-selected and K-selected traits
Generalists, because they lay eggs on beaches

why.correct: r and K are ends of a range; many species mix traits.
options: Their long life and late breeding are K-selected traits.
Many eggs and no care are r-selected traits.
Right: many eggs and no care are r-like; long life and late breeding are K-like.
Generalist describes niche width, not reproductive strategy.

items.q: A town sprays a field heavily with a chemical to kill insect pests on its crops, and the spray also kills a population of insect-eating birds. Which outcome is most likely over the next few years?
options: The birds return first and keep the pest numbers low
Neither returns, because the spray poisons the field for good
The pests and the birds return at about the same rate
Pests return faster than birds, so damage can be worse

why.correct: A disruption that hits both an r-selected pest and its slower-breeding predator favors the pest.
options: Birds that raise few young a year recover more slowly than insects.
Both can return; the question is which is faster.
Their reproductive strategies differ, so their recovery rates differ.
Right: r-selected insects rebound quickly; K-like birds, raising few young, take longer to recover.
